entry.title: automated-release
entry.content:
A tik process with 3 stages

Identity

A definition is named by its content, so this address is what a ticket pins and what a consumer checks against:

sha256-c1cffcb2e879ff82ad36bf8e67c993aa8ddb0c5caacbdd484ec8440cb549c8bb

Shape

● built ★        ⊢ version · commit · ✎ci · ⧉checksums/
│
├─▶ attested ★   ⊢ artifact.digest · ✎ci · ⊙sbom · ⊙provenance
└─▶ scanned ★    ⊢ scan.result = clean · ✎ci · ⊙vulnerability-scan

Roles to fill

Every role ships empty, so adopting a process never inherits somebody else’s org chart. Name yours with tik roles add <role> <actor>.

  • ci — empty

Facts it records

Path Shape
artifact.digest [:string {:min 8}]
commit [:string {:min 7}]
scan.result [:enum :clean :findings]
version [:string {:min 1}]

Stages

built · sticky

Once reached it stays reached: the fold carries it forward, so later evidence cannot take it away.

Reached when:

  • the fact version stands
  • the fact commit stands
  • commit was asserted by a member of the ci role
  • an artifact is attached whose path starts with checksums/

Runbook: kb/runbooks/automated-release-built.md

attested · sticky

Follows built.

Once reached it stays reached: the fold carries it forward, so later evidence cannot take it away.

Reached when:

  • the fact artifact.digest stands
  • artifact.digest was asserted by a member of the ci role
  • an attestation of :sbom exists, no older than P1D
  • an attestation of :provenance exists, no older than P1D

Runbook: kb/runbooks/automated-release-attested.md

scanned · sticky

Follows built.

Once reached it stays reached: the fold carries it forward, so later evidence cannot take it away.

Reached when:

  • the fact scan.result equals :clean
  • scan.result was asserted by a member of the ci role
  • an attestation of :vulnerability-scan exists, no older than P1D

Runbook: kb/runbooks/automated-release-scanned.md

Take it

tik adopt processes/automated-release.edn```

The definition and its runbooks are copied into your store, and the
publisher's signature travels with them when a key in your `actors`
verifies it.

Read the stages before you adopt: they say who has to sign what,
which is a decision about your organisation.

entry.title: Bundle format
entry.content:
tik-evidence-bundle version 1 — the on-disk contract, the checks a reader runs, and the rules that govern change.

tik-evidence-bundle, version 1. A gzipped tar holding one ticket and everything its derivation needs.

tik bundle <id> --out evidence.tgz

bundle.edn                          the format name and version
actors                              the allowed-signers registry
pq-signers                          the ML-DSA-65 key registry, where the store keeps one
signatures.edn                      the signature policy, where the store sets one
roles.edn                           role membership, where the store keeps a register
delegation.edn                      the store's delegation policy, where it sets one
identity/<event-id>.edn             key bindings and delegations, as signed registry events
identity/<event-id>.sig.<fpr>       their authorship signatures
identity/keys/<kid>.pem             the issuer keys those bindings rest on
processes/by-hash/<hash>.edn        the definition the ticket pinned
processes/by-hash/<hash>.sig.<fpr>  its publication signatures
tickets/<uuid>/events/<id>.edn      the append-only log
tickets/<uuid>/events/<id>.sig.<fpr>      authorship signatures
tickets/<uuid>/events/<id>.pqsig.<fpr>    post-quantum authorship signatures
tickets/<uuid>/events/<id>.witness.<fpr>  countersignatures over a head
tickets/<uuid>/events/<id>.pqwitness.<fpr>  ML-DSA-65 countersignatures sealing an ancestry
tickets/<uuid>/blobs/<hash>         attached artifacts, addressed by content
verify.sh                           a coreutils implementation of the checks
README.md                           what the recipient is holding

What a reader may assume

Every stored file’s name is the SHA-256 of its bytes, prefixed sha256-. Event and definition files carry a .edn suffix after the address; blobs are named by the bare address. sha256sum alone audits the archive.

Event bytes are exactly the hashed region. An event file holds the canonical serialization without its :event/id, because the filename is the id. Re-emitting a parsed event reproduces the file byte for byte.

Signatures are detached siblings. <id>.sig.<fingerprint> covers the event’s stored bytes under the tik-event namespace; <id>.witness.<fpr> covers a head under tik-witness; a definition’s .sig.<fpr> uses tik-process. Each verifies with ssh-keygen -Y verify against actors. <id>.pqsig.<fpr> is the raw FIPS 204 ML-DSA-65 signature over the bytes tik-event-v1, a NUL byte, then the event’s stored bytes, by the pq-signers key whose DER SubjectPublicKeyInfo hashes (SHA-256, hex) to <fpr>.

Exactly one ticket directory, with exactly one root event. Every parent an event names is present in the same directory, so the Merkle DAG the log commits to is complete.

The pinned definition travels. The create event carries :ticket/process-hash, and processes/by-hash/<that hash>.edn holds the definition whose content address equals it.

identity/ holds excerpts. A key binding travels as the single registry event that made it, with its own authorship signature and the issuer’s public key. Its parents live in a registry ticket that stays behind, so its standing rests on its content address plus the issuer’s signature over the id-token it carries.

Delegations travel with the verdicts they cover. A verdict signed by the throwaway key of a tik review --batch (ADR 0037) counts only through the delegation that names the key, so the bundle carries every delegation covering one of its events, and delegation.edn ({:require-touch true} or false) when the store sets a delegation policy. A bundle without delegation.edn credits delegations without a touch requirement, as a store without a policy does.

The role register travels where the store keeps one. roles.edn maps each role to its members in the shape a definition declares, {:role {:members ["actor" …]} …}, and replaces the definition’s members role by role. A bundle without roles.edn re-derives under the definition’s members, as a store without a register does. A roles.edn that is present and does not parse, does not have that shape, or is not a regular file makes the bundle unreadable: a reader refuses it rather than fall back to the definition’s members, because the register is how a member’s departure is expressed. The file carries no content address and no signature, so it states the membership the producing store held without proving it.

bundle.edn declares the packaging version and nothing else. The ticket, the head, the definition and the stage are derivable from the files, so the manifest names none of them and nothing in it is trusted. A bundle without a manifest is version 1.

The checks

These are what the format promises. verify.sh implements them with coreutils, ssh-keygen and — for key bindings — openssl; tik rederive implements them in process. The script travels inside the archive it checks, so read it before you run it, or run this list yourself.

  1. Integrity. Every tickets/*/events/*.edn, identity/*.edn, processes/by-hash/*.edn and tickets/*/blobs/* hashes to its own name.
  2. Shape. Exactly one ticket directory.
  3. Completeness. Every parent referenced by an event is present, and exactly one event has empty :event/parents.
  4. Authorship. Every .sig. sidecar verifies as the actor its own event names — binding -I to :event/actor rather than accepting whoever happened to sign, so a registered actor cannot sign another’s authorship. Every .pqsig. sidecar likewise verifies as its event’s actor through a pq-signers line that allows the tik-event namespace. A .pqsig. sidecar without pq-signers fails, and verify.sh fails one it cannot check because the host’s OpenSSL is older than 3.5. A .sig. sidecar whose key actors does not grant still counts when a delegation in identity/ covers it:
    • the delegation is an attestation by the event’s actor, verifying through an actors line no key binding earned, and touched where delegation.edn requires it;
    • its window is at most five minutes and holds the event’s :event/at;
    • its scope names the event’s ticket together with one of the event’s parents;
    • its facts name the path the event asserts;
    • the sidecar verifies against the key the delegation names.
  5. Countersignature. Every .witness. sidecar verifies as a registered principal under tik-witness. Every .pqwitness. sidecar is an ML-DSA-65 signature over tik-witness-v1\0 followed by the event’s bytes, by a pq-signers key allowed tik-witness.
  6. Signature policy. Where signatures.edn travels, it reads as {:require #{:ssh-ed25519 …} :from <instant>} over the algorithms :ssh-ed25519 and :ml-dsa-65, or the bundle fails. Every event carries a verifying ssh-ed25519 signature by its actor; from :from on, also one for every other required algorithm; and where :ml-dsa-65 is required, every event claimed before :from is a .pqwitness. event or one of its ancestors.
  7. Key bindings. For each binding in identity/: the issuer signed the id-token, using the key at identity/keys/<kid>.pem; the token’s sub and iss equal the binding’s; the token was live at the binding’s :event/at; the token names the key it binds, as a nonce or an aud suffix equal to tik-key-<sha256 of the key> (ADR 0035); and the key it binds appears in actors.

Check 7 is checkable offline because the issuer’s key travels in the archive, and it says exactly this much: whoever built this bundle holds a token that this key signed, for this subject and this bound key, at that moment. Recognizing the key as the issuer’s is the reader’s job, the same way recognizing an actors line is — a subject like repo:metio/tik:ref:refs/heads/main is worth what the reader knows about that repository and that IdP.

An unsigned event is authenticity unclaimed rather than a failure, and a binding whose issuer key is absent grants nothing and is reported as such. Everything else in the list is a failure.

Deriving the ticket’s stages needs the definition as well, which is where tik rederive goes on and verify.sh stops.

Compatibility

Version 1 is the layout above. The rules below are what a reader written against it may rely on.

A reader ignores what it does not recognize. Unknown files, directories and manifest keys are passed over. That is what makes the additions in the next paragraph safe.

These may appear without a version bump:

  • new top-level files and directories;
  • new files inside existing directories, including new sidecar kinds (<id>.<kind>.<fingerprint>);
  • new keys in bundle.edn;
  • new event types, fact paths, guard operators and process keys inside the files, which are versioned by the kernel’s own vocabularies rather than by this format;
  • any change to verify.sh and README.md, which carry no contract of their own.

These force a version bump:

  • moving, renaming or removing anything the layout names;
  • changing what a name means — a different hash function, a different suffix convention, a signature namespace;
  • changing the canonical serialization, which changes every event id and is versioned separately by tik.canonical/format-version;
  • carrying more than one ticket;
  • anything else that makes a conforming version-1 reader compute a different answer or fail.

A reader holding a bundle whose major version it does not know declines it and says so.

Reading a bundle yourself

The archive unpacks to plain files, so an implementation in any language is a hash, a signature check and an EDN reader.

mkdir bundle && tar xzf evidence.tgz -C bundle && cd bundle

# 1. integrity, without any tool of ours
sha256sum tickets/*/events/*.edn | while read sum f; do
  [ "sha256-$sum" = "$(basename "$f" .edn)" ] || echo "MISMATCH $f"
done

# 2. authorship, as the actor each event names
for sig in tickets/*/events/*.sig.*; do
  ev="${sig%%.sig.*}.edn"
  actor=$(sed -n 's/^{:event\/actor "\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$ev")
  ssh-keygen -Y verify -f actors -I "$actor" -n tik-event -s "$sig" < "$ev"
done

Canonical bytes sort map keys, so :event/actor always leads an event file — which is why one sed finds it.

Relationship to in-toto

in-toto attestations describe a build: this subject, this predicate, signed by this functionary. A bundle carries a different kind of thing — the facts, the rules that judge them, and the means to recompute the verdict offline. in-toto’s nearest analogue is the layout, and a tik process definition already is one.

The two compose. tik bridge intoto reads a SLSA provenance, an SPDX or CycloneDX SBOM, or a vulnerability report into an attestation event, so an :attested-within guard is satisfied by the format your pipeline already emits, and the result travels in a bundle.

entry.title: Claude Code skill
entry.content:
Install the tik skill so Claude drives a store correctly — recording evidence and letting stages derive, instead of setting statuses.

Install the tik skill into Claude Code and Claude gains working knowledge of tik: it recognises a store, records facts with tik set rather than inventing a status field, reads tik explain before asking a person anything, and authors process definitions whose stages derive from evidence instead of listing activities.

That last part is the reason the skill exists. The failure mode for any model writing a tik process is a task list wearing a process costume — stages named after activities, with nothing following from anything. The skill carries the design law that rules it out, along with the closed guard vocabulary and the authoring loop that checks the result.

The skill lives in this repository under skills/tik/, packaged as a Claude Code plugin by the manifests in .claude-plugin/.

Install

Add this repository as a plugin marketplace, then install the plugin:

/plugin marketplace add metio/tik
/plugin install tik@tik

Claude activates the skill whenever a repository holds a tickets/ or .tik/ directory, an actors registry, or processes/*.edn — or when you mention tik, tickets, processes, or stages.

From the MCP server

A tik MCP server also serves the skill, through the MCP Skills extension (io.modelcontextprotocol/skills). With the server registered, Claude Code v2.1.331 or later lists the skill as <server>:tik, for example tik:tik, and loads the copy built into that server, so it matches the server’s version without a plugin install. Claude Code lists MCP skills only over MCP revision 2026-07-28, which tik mcp and tik serve speak. See MCP server for how the manifest is signed and checked.

What it grants Claude

The skill teaches the CLI surface and the model behind it:

  • The daily loop — tik ls, tik next, tik new, tik set, tik explain, tik status, and the selector grammar for filtering a board.
  • Corrections — retract, dispute, and the fact that a dispute is answered only by a different value, so Claude does not try to clear one by retyping the same fact.
  • Authoring — tik author, the guard vocabulary, and the lint, simulate, and test loop that proves a definition before a real ticket depends on it.
  • The one design law — a stage is defined by what must be TRUE to reach it, never by who moved what.

It also knows when not to act: an unreachable step in explain means waiting is pointless and the definition or the role register needs fixing, not patience.

Hearing about changes

tik notify runs a local notifier that re-derives and verifies every ticket whose log changed and pushes a hint of each stage change to the sessions that asked for it, over a Unix socket only your user can reach:

tik notify --config ~/.config/tik/notify.edn

{:stores {"metio" "~/git/github.com/metio/.tik"}
 :window "PT5S"
 :sinks [{:store "metio" :where "stage=:asked"
          :command ["notify-send" "tik" "{line}"]}]}

A Claude Code session subscribes by running tik notify watch under the Monitor tool, which feeds each output line back to Claude:

tik notify watch --store metio --where "fact:request.from=infra.run"

Each line is one JSON hint naming the store, the ticket, its title, the stages it left and entered, and the actor of the event that moved it. A hint holds no fact values and is never evidence: Claude re-derives with tik status before acting on it. tik notify channel delivers the same hints as a Claude Code channel to a session started with --dangerously-load-development-channels server:<name>. The channel speaks only the legacy initialize handshake and answers server/discover with -32601. It reads at most 1 MiB per stdin line, like tik mcp: a longer line, or one that is not valid JSON, answers a parse error (-32700) whose data.rule names the rule, and the next line is read. Hints sent while nobody was subscribed are not replayed, so keep a slow fallback poll. The decisions behind this are in ADR 0040 .

For agents generally

The skill is one surface over a derivation every tool can read. The gated agent commands enforce the same boundary without any prompt-side cooperation:

tik agent actions 3184 --actor bot
tik agent set 3184 severity=:high --actor bot

An agent sees only what the frontier admits for its role, and anything else is refused with the derived reason. Because the boundary is the derivation rather than an instruction, it cannot be talked around.

This site also publishes /llms.txt and /llms-full.txt, so a model can read the documentation directly.

entry.title: Clojure library
entry.content:
Read, verify and derive one ticket of a store in process with tik.api, read-only and without starting a process.

tik.api gives a JVM, babashka or native-image program the answers of tik status and tik verify for one ticket without running the CLI. It never writes to the store, signs, runs a probe, touches the network or starts a process.

(require '[tik.api :as api])

(def store (api/open-store "/path/to/.tik"))   ; the dir holding tickets/ or tik.db

(api/derive store "f106aa78")
;; => {:ticket #uuid "f106aa78-…" :title "…"
;;     :rules {:process :skilled-change :version 2 :hash "sha256-…"}
;;     :current [:scoped] :reached [:scoped]
;;     :facts {[:kind] {:status :present :value :feat :by "claude"} …}
;;     :missing-parents nil
;;     :definition {:pinned "sha256-…" :derived-under "sha256-…" :source :archive}
;;     :at #inst "…"}

(:ok? (api/verify-ticket store "f106aa78"))

Add tik as a git dependency in deps.edn:

{:deps {io.github.metio/tik {:git/sha "<commit>"}}}

The calls

  • (open-store root) or (open-store root {:limits {…}}) opens the store whose root is root, the directory holding tickets/ (file store) or tik.db (SQLite store). Nothing is discovered from parent directories.
  • (resolve-id store ref) takes a uuid, the full id, or a prefix of at least 8 characters naming exactly one ticket.
  • (ticket store ref) returns the ticket’s events in reduction order.
  • (derive store ref {:at instant}) returns the ticket’s title, rules, current and reached stages and facts. They equal what tik status <id> --edn --at <instant> prints. When the definition found in the store does not hash to the ticket’s pin, derive refuses unless {:allow-unpinned-definition true} is passed.
  • (verify-ticket store ref) runs the tik verify ladder for that ticket with the same code as the CLI and returns it as data: :ok?, :failures, one summary per event (:integrity and :signature, which is :verified, :delegated, :unsigned, :unchecked or :failed) and every check as an item.

tik.api/version is the contract’s version; it changes only when a documented key, argument or refusal changes meaning or goes away.

Refusals

Every refusal is an ex-info whose :type is in the tik.api namespace: not-a-store, ambiguous-store, backend-unavailable, invalid-argument, invalid-id, unknown-ticket, ambiguous-id (with :candidates), too-large (with :limit and :actual), unreadable, definition-missing, definition-mismatch, malformed-roles, underivable and read-only.

Differences from the CLI

  • Signatures are verified in process (Ed25519, Ed25519 security keys, ML-DSA-65). A key type only ssh-keygen reads is :unchecked, and its check fails where tik verify would ask ssh-keygen.
  • Every event, sidecar and config file is measured before it is read, and a symbolic link inside a ticket directory is refused. The defaults are tik.api/default-limits.
  • A SQLite store is opened read-only and needs the SQLite driver, which babashka lacks. A native image that reads SQLite stores or identity bindings must require tik.store.sqlite-jdbc or cheshire.core at build time.

The reasoning is recorded in ADR 0044 .

entry.title: Derived beats declared
entry.content:
The one law — if something follows from the log, storing it as authoritative state is a bug.

If something can be derived, storing it as authoritative state is a bug. That is the whole law, and every design question in tik resolves against it.

A ticket’s stage is the obvious case. It is never written down anywhere. It is f(events, now) — a pure function of the ticket’s own event log, the process definition that ticket pinned, and the instant you are asking about. Ask twice with the same inputs and you get the same answer, forever.

What the law buys

Correctness by construction. A stored status can disagree with the facts; a derived one cannot. When somebody retracts the approval that a ticket’s :approved stage depended on, the stage regresses on the next read, with no rollback step, no cleanup job, and no window during which the board is lying.

Every question about every moment. Because now is an argument rather than an ambient clock, “what was true on March 1” is answered by evaluating March 1:

tik status 3184 --at 2026-03-01T00:00:00Z

Replication without coordination. There is no authoritative mutable cell to serialize behind a lock, so replicas merge by unioning their event sets and each derives the same answer independently. See Replication .

Auditability that survives the tool. The conclusion is reproducible from the signed bytes by anyone, including someone who does not run tik. tik bundle packs one ticket into a tarball that verifies with coreutils and ssh-keygen alone, and tik rederive recomputes the stages it implies from the rules travelling inside it. See Evidence .

What the law costs

Derivation is work done on every read, and the law forbids the obvious shortcut of remembering the answer. tik pays that cost deliberately and keeps it bounded: the fold is linear in events and polynomial in the size of the process definition, which is authored and small. Fact lookups are served from indexes the fold maintains, so history length does not turn into a quadratic.

Performance problems get indexes, caches, or a different storage backend. They never get new authoritative state. A cache that some lens keeps is fine as long as nothing treats it as the truth — the truth is recomputed from the events.

The companion law

Coordination-free by construction: no leader, no lock, no consensus. Every operation is correct on arbitrarily many replicas that share nothing and reconcile only by eventually unioning their grow-only, content-addressed event sets.

Reads consult one ticket’s own log, so they shard without limit. Writes are either content-addressed events that are a pure function of their intent — two replicas forming the same intent emit byte-identical events, and the union keeps one — or appends whose contention resolves by derivation: two competing claims about a fact reduce to :conflicted, a derived state, rather than a lock to be won.

A design that needs a replica to win an election, hold a lock, or agree with a quorum before it can act breaks this law as surely as caching a derived value breaks the first one.

What the kernel refuses to answer

The kernel answers “what follows from these signed facts?” It never answers “what should happen next?” There are no workflow transitions, no scheduler, no policy engine, and no external queries in the core. A guard consults one ticket’s log and nothing else — never a service, never another ticket, never a clock of its own.

Notifications, inboxes, webhooks, boards, and agent surfaces are all porcelain over derivations. That boundary is what keeps evaluation offline, reproducible, and true years from now.

entry.title: employee-onboarding
entry.content:
A tik process template with 4 stages

What you choose

tik adopt reads these from the template itself and asks for each one, typed and validated — no EDN to hand-write.

Question Answer
with-equipment :boolean does someone hand over equipment? (optional)
with-accounts :boolean does someone provision accounts? (optional)
with-buddy :boolean is a named buddy required before day one counts? (optional)

Identity

Your answers decide this one: turn a stage off and the process is a different process with a different address. The shape below is what employee-onboarding.params.edn produces, with every option on:

sha256-95c7eadc7481ddec6ed5db85ac555e9302d6d7e2c9bc82505e767c8628de0f23

Every option on. Stages that depend on an answer say so below.

● hired             ⊢ start-date · ⧉contract/ · ✎hr
│
├─▶ equipped        ⊢ ✎it
│   │
│   ┈▶ ready
└─▶ accounts-live   ⊢ ✎it
    │
    ▼ ready ★       ⊢ ⋈ after equipped, accounts-live   buddy

Every role ships empty, so adopting a process never inherits somebody else’s org chart. Name yours with tik roles add <role> <actor>.

buddy [:string {:min 2}]

Stages

hired

Reached when:

  • the fact start-date stands
  • an artifact is attached whose path starts with contract/
  • contract.ref was asserted by a member of the hr role

Runbook: kb/runbooks/onboarding-hired.md

equipped

Included when you answer yes to with-equipment.

Follows hired.

Reached when:

  • equipment.ref was asserted by a member of the it role

Runbook: kb/runbooks/onboarding-equipped.md

accounts-live

Included when you answer yes to with-accounts.

Follows hired.

Reached when:

  • accounts.email was asserted by a member of the it role

Runbook: kb/runbooks/onboarding-accounts.md

ready · sticky

Follows equipped, accounts-live.

Reached when:

  • the fact buddy stands

Runbook: kb/runbooks/onboarding-ready.md

Take it

entry.title: Events and facts
entry.content:
Seven event types, five fact statuses, and the content addressing that makes a store auditable with coreutils.

A ticket is an append-only set of events. Everything else about it is computed.

Seven event types

The vocabulary is closed and versioned, because the semantics of a verifiable kernel have to be enumerable:

Event Meaning
:ticket/create the ticket exists, pinned to a process definition by hash
:fact/assert a claim about a path: [:severity] = :high
:fact/retract withdraw a claim, with no replacement
:fact/dispute reject a claim, with a reason
:artifact/attach a file, stored and addressed by its hash
:attestation/add a signed claim the kernel does not interpret
:process/migrate re-pin this ticket to a newer definition

Things that look like they need their own type turn out not to. Comments are artifacts — text blobs attached by hash. Links are facts under a [:link …] path. Work records are :work attestation claims. Witness countersignatures are detached sidecars over a head rather than events, because an event would move the very head it witnesses.

Content addressing

An event’s id is the SHA-256 of its canonical bytes, and the stored file is named for that id. The bytes on disk are exactly the hashed region, so a store audits with nothing but coreutils:

sha256sum tickets/*/events/*.edn   # filename must equal the digest

Signatures never live inside the hashed region. They are detached sidecars alongside the event, which is what lets a second person add their signature to an event without changing its identity.

Every event names its parents, forming a Merkle DAG. Parents carry integrity and causality — they are how a replica knows whether two writes saw each other. They never carry ordering: the fold orders by (at, id) over the event set, which is what makes the reducer total, commutative, and idempotent.

Fact status

One function decides why a fact does or does not satisfy a guard, and guards consult nothing else:

Status Meaning
:present a value stands
:absent nothing has been claimed
:retracted withdrawn, no replacement offered
:disputed rejected with a reason, and unusable until corrected
:conflicted causally concurrent claims disagree

What a dispute means

A dispute rejects the value that stood when it was raised: the latest claim on the path among the dispute’s own ancestors, which is the value its author saw. A concurrent correction the disputer had not seen is not what they rejected, so it is not held hostage by the dispute. The assertion that answers a dispute has to claim something else. Re-asserting the rejected value verbatim leaves the path :disputed — otherwise the party a dispute holds accountable could clear it in one command by retyping the same fact.

A retraction leaves the path :retracted, because the rejected claim is gone, but it does not answer the dispute: asserting the rejected value again after the retraction leaves the path :disputed, exactly as a direct re-assertion would. A dispute raised on a path holding nothing rejects no particular value, so the first assertion answers it, which is what keeps a dispute from making a path permanently unusable.

Disputes accumulate: several people may reject the same claim, and each withdraws only their own.

tik dispute 3184 category --reason "this is billing, not technical"
tik dispute 3184 category --withdraw     # takes back your own objection

What a conflict means

When two replicas write the same path without having seen each other, and they disagree, the fact reads :conflicted and every guard that depends on it fails with a reason saying so. Nobody has to win. A later write that observed both supersedes them, and the conflict resolves by derivation.

Concurrent writes that happen to agree are not a conflict — there is no disagreement to surface.

entry.title: Explain
entry.content:
The product surface — what evidence is missing, who may supply it, and when waiting is pointless.

A traditional tracker exposes state. tik exposes justification: what is true, why it is true, and what evidence is missing next. tik explain is where that surfaces, and every other view is a rendering of it.

$ tik explain 3184
To reach :resolved:
  ✓ [:fact [:resolution :ref]]
  ✗ attach an artifact whose path starts with "repro/"
  blocks: :closed
  (see: kb/runbooks/support-request-resolved.md)

Nothing in that block is speculation. The checkmarks are guards that already hold, the crosses are structured reasons produced by guard evaluation, blocks is the downstream closure, and the hint is the runbook the definition declares for that stage.

Reasons are data

The prose lives in this lens only. Underneath, each missing step is a structured reason carrying the path, the schema, the role, the actor whose signature already counted — whatever the guard knows:

tik explain 3184 --edn

That data contract is stable plumbing; the English is not. It renders as CLI text, as web forms built from the schemas in the reasons, and as agent task specifications whose acceptance criteria are the guards.

Reasons are sorted by who can act on them right now: values anyone can supply first, then corrections, artifacts, specific people, attestations, other stages, and finally time, which is nobody’s to act on.

Who can act

--actor filters a block to what one person can do, and counts the rest rather than hiding it:

$ tik explain 3184 --actor alice
To reach :resolved:
  ✗ attach an artifact whose path starts with "repro/"
  … 1 step(s) waiting on others or time

tik next rotates the same derivation into an inbox — for a person, or for a whole role:

tik next --actor alice
tik next --role :triager

The inbox ranks by unlock impact, so the step that frees the most downstream work comes first, and it holds back tickets whose dependency links point at unsettled upstream work. Steps toward a stage that needs a present fact changed, the branch a ticket did not take, are labelled with the fact they would replace and listed after the forward steps.

Waiting versus impossible

Some blocked tickets are waiting for a colleague. Others can never move at all — a role with no members, a negation over a sticky stage already reached, a prerequisite that is itself dead. Those look identical until you say so, and telling somebody to wait for something that will never arrive is the failure that matters most for a tool whose whole claim is answering what is blocking.

$ tik explain 9c21
To reach :approved (unreachable):
  ⊘ fact [:sign-off] must be asserted by a member of role :auditor
      (currently by "seb") — nobody can ever do this

The derivation stays conservative: a step is only called impossible when it is provably undischargeable from the definition and the log. A choice dies only when every one of its branches does. Anything merely waiting keeps its ✗.

Proving it

tik causal answers the auditor’s question — which signed events made each reached stage true, with negations and time saying so honestly:

tik causal 3184

And tik whatif asks the counterfactual without writing anything:

tik whatif 3184 severity=:low +P2D retract:category

entry.title: GitHub Actions
entry.content:
Failed workflow runs as ci-failure tickets, one per failure streak.
tik bridge github --config github.edn             # poll once
tik bridge github --config github.edn --webhook   # serve workflow_run deliveries

tik bridge github turns failed GitHub Actions runs into tickets under the ci-failure process. One ticket covers one failure streak: the consecutive failed runs of one workflow on one branch, from the first failure after a green run up to the next green run. Further failures attach to the open ticket as ci/run/<id>/<attempt> artifacts, the next green run is recorded as forge.green-run, and a failure after that opens a new ticket. Cancelled, skipped and neutral runs neither extend nor end a streak. GitLab pipelines feed the same process with the same facts, so the metrics below cover both forges.

Configuration

{:repos   ["metio/tik" {:repo "metio/jaas" :branches ["main" "next"]}]
 :orgs    ["metio" "sebhoss"]       ; every non-archived repository, default branch
 :exclude ["metio/scratch"]
 :token   {:env "GITHUB_TOKEN"}     ; or {:command …} / {:file …} / {:credential …}
 :tokens  {"sebhoss" {:command ["pass" "show" "github/sebhoss"]}}
 :api     "https://api.github.com"  ; a GitHub Enterprise Server URL also works
 :actor   "github"
 :actions {:process   :ci-failure
           :lookback  "P14D"        ; streaks with no run newer than this are left alone
           :max-pages 5             ; history pages fetched to find a streak's first run
           :failing   #{"failure" "timed_out" "startup_failure"}
           :green     #{"success"}}
 :webhook {:secret {:env "GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET"} :port 8787}}

Each source is enabled by its block; :actions is the only source so far. A token needs read access to Actions and metadata on the repositories it covers. :tokens maps a repository owner to its own token, because a fine-grained GitHub token is scoped to one resource owner; owners without an entry use :token, then $GITHUB_TOKEN. An :orgs entry may also name a user account: its public repositories are listed, plus its private ones when that owner’s token belongs to the user. A failure listing one owner is reported and skips that owner only.

The bridge actor (github by default) must be registered in actors with the key in TIK_KEY. The ci-failure process’s :bridge role holds only the forge bridges (github, gitlab), so nobody else can open or recover a streak.

Each ticket records forge.host, forge.repo, forge.owner, forge.workflow, forge.branch, forge.first-run and forge.head-sha, plus repo, the repository’s name as a keyword (:tik): the value tik new records for a ticket made inside the checkout. A store above many checkouts therefore shows a repository’s CI failures next to its other tickets (tik ls --all --where 'fact:repo=:tik').

Polling and webhooks

Both drivers run the same sync and are idempotent, so they can run side by side and on several replicas. A ticket id hashes the repository id, workflow, branch and first failed run. A ticket is dated by the creation time of its first failed run, and each later event by the start time of the run attempt it records. GitHub never changes either timestamp, whereas it does rewrite updated_at on old runs. Two replicas syncing the same history therefore write identical events, and a re-poll writes nothing. Time to :recovered runs from the first failed run’s creation to the start of the green run.

Run both from tik backend (pipelines.edn):

{:pipelines
 [{:id :github-poll    :every "PT10M" :run ["bridge" "github"] :as "github"}
  {:id :github-webhook :watch true    :run ["bridge" "github" "--webhook"] :as "github"}]}

For the webhook, point a repository or organization webhook at the listener with content type application/json, the shared secret, and the Workflow runs event. Deliveries without a valid X-Hub-Signature-256 are refused with 401. A delivery only names the workflow; the bridge then reads that workflow’s history from the API, so a lost delivery is repaired by the next poll.

A streak whose first run lies beyond :max-pages of history is skipped with a message instead of being opened on a guessed start, because a guessed start would give replicas different ticket ids.

Triage

The cause is the one fact the forge cannot supply:

tik set <id> cause=dependency   # flaky | code | dependency | config | infra | upstream

A ticket reaches :resolved once it has both a cause and a bridge-signed green run.

Metrics

tik stats groups any tickets by a fact and derives the counts and the time from creation to a stage:

tik stats --by forge.repo --split cause --until :resolved --where 'fact:forge.workflow'
tik stats --by forge.host --until :recovered
tik stats --by forge.repo --format json

The columns are the ticket count, how many have not reached the stage, and the median, 90th-percentile and mean time to reach it. The fact:forge.workflow term restricts the count to CI-failure tickets. Every number is recomputed from the ticket logs on each run.

entry.title: GitLab pipelines
entry.content:
Failed GitLab pipelines as ci-failure tickets, one per failure streak, optionally through an SSH port forward.
tik bridge gitlab --config gitlab.edn   # poll once

tik bridge gitlab turns failed GitLab pipelines into ci-failure tickets, with the same streak rules, facts and metrics as GitHub Actions . A pipeline has no workflow id; its source (push, schedule, web, …) takes that place, so a failing nightly schedule and green push pipelines on the same branch are separate streaks, titled push pipeline, schedule pipeline and so on. Pipelines with any status other than failed and success (canceled, skipped, manual) neither extend nor end a streak.

Configuration

{:url        "https://gitlab.example"   ; the web URL; the API is <url>/api/v4
 :membership true                       ; every project the token's account is a member of
 :groups     ["team/platform"]          ; every project of a group and its subgroups
 :projects   ["team/app" {:project "team/lib" :branches ["main" "next"]}]
 :exclude    ["team/platform/scratch"]
 :token      {:env "GITLAB_TOKEN"}      ; or {:command …} / {:file …} / {:credential …}
 :tunnel     {:ssh "admin@gitlab.example" :target "127.0.0.1:8080"}
 :actor      "gitlab"
 :pipelines  {:process   :ci-failure
              :lookback  "P14D"
              :max-pages 5
              :failing   #{"failed"}
              :green     #{"success"}}}

The token needs read access to the API (read_api). Archived projects are left out, and a project without :branches watches its default branch. A failure listing one group or project is reported and skips it only.

SSH port forward

Some GitLab instances only serve their API on the host itself. With :tunnel, the bridge runs ssh -N -L 127.0.0.1:<free port>:<target> <ssh> for the duration of the sweep and sends the API requests to the local end. The forwarded target speaks plain HTTP; the connection that leaves the machine is the SSH one. Outside a tunnel, the bridge refuses a non-HTTPS API URL. The SSH destination must be an account allowed to forward ports, and ssh runs with BatchMode=yes, so its key must be usable without a prompt (an agent or an unencrypted key).

Retried pipelines

A retried pipeline keeps its id and shows only its latest outcome, so the bridge checks every green pipeline for a ticket opened on it and records the recovery there. GitLab’s pipeline list carries no start time, so such a recovery is dated by the pipeline’s creation and its time to :recovered reads as zero.
